questions.enonce_markdown:
What do you understand by an optimum population?

(4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The size of a country's population is judged against its resources, so economists speak of an *optimum* population.

**Definition.** An **optimum population** is the size of population which, with the **existing natural resources, capital and level of technology**, produces the **maximum output (income) per head**, that is the **highest standard of living** for the people.

**Explanation.**
- **Under-population**: the population is **smaller** than the optimum. Resources (land, minerals, forests) are not fully used, there is a shortage of labour, and output per head is below its maximum. Adding people would raise output per head.
- **Over-population**: the population is **larger** than the optimum. There are too many people for the available resources, so extra workers add little (diminishing returns), unemployment and poverty appear, and output per head falls.
- At the **optimum**, output per head is at its **peak**. This point is **not fixed**: it moves when resources are discovered, when capital is accumulated or when technology improves.

![fig-1](gce-ol-economics-2021-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)

**Conclusion.** An optimum population is therefore the population size that gives the highest output per head for the resources, capital and technology available at a given time.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The population of a country in 2010 was 24 million inhabitants, comprising 30% youths, 60% in the working age group and 10% in the old age group. The total output for the year was valued at 480 million FCFA. Calculate:

(i) The size of the dependent population. (4 marks)

(ii) The dependency ratio. (2 marks)

(iii) The per capita income. (2 marks)

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Size of the dependent population (4 marks)**

The **dependent population** is made up of the people who are **not of working age**: the youths and the old.

- Share of dependants $= 30\% + 10\% = 40\%$ of the population.
- Youths: $\dfrac{30}{100} \times 24\,000\,000 = 7\,200\,000$
- Old people: $\dfrac{10}{100} \times 24\,000\,000 = 2\,400\,000$
- **Dependent population** $= 7\,200\,000 + 2\,400\,000 = $ **9 600 000 people** (9.6 million).

(The working population is $60\% \times 24\,000\,000 = 14\,400\,000$ people.)

**(ii) Dependency ratio (2 marks)**

$$\text{Dependency ratio} = \frac{\text{dependent population}}{\text{working population}} \times 100$$

$$= \frac{9\,600\,000}{14\,400\,000} \times 100 = 66.67\% \approx 66.7\%$$

Equivalently $40 : 60 = 2 : 3$, or about $0.67$. **Every 100 workers support about 67 dependants** (every 3 workers support 2 dependants).

**(iii) Per capita income (2 marks)**

$$\text{Per capita income} = \frac{\text{total output (national income)}}{\text{population}}$$

$$= \frac{480\,000\,000 \text{ FCFA}}{24\,000\,000 \text{ people}} = \textbf{20 FCFA per person}$$

*Note.* The figures are those of the question; the value obtained is very small only because the output given is small compared with the population.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Explain four effects of a large scale emigration of Cameroonians of the age range 18 to 60 years on the economy of Cameroon.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Cameroonians aged 18 to 60 are the **working-age population**: they work, pay taxes and consume. Large-scale emigration of this group therefore affects the economy in several ways, some harmful and some favourable.

**1. Fall in the labour force and in output.** Many farmers, craftsmen, traders and workers leave. The labour supply shrinks, so firms and farms (cocoa, coffee, banana plantations) lack workers, production falls and the growth of national income slows down. Labour shortages can also push wages up and raise production costs.

**2. Brain drain: loss of skilled workers.** Doctors, teachers, engineers and technicians are among those who emigrate. The State spent money training them, and that investment is lost to another country. Hospitals, schools and industries are left without enough skilled workers, which lowers the quality of services and productivity.

**3. Higher dependency ratio and heavier burden on those who remain.** The working population becomes smaller, while the number of children and old people to support is unchanged. Each remaining worker supports more dependants, and the **government's tax revenue falls** (fewer income earners), reducing its ability to finance roads, schools and hospitals.

**4. Remittances and relief from unemployment (favourable effects).** Emigrants send money home, which brings **foreign exchange**, improves the balance of payments and raises family incomes and consumption. Emigration also reduces **unemployment and pressure on jobs** at home, and some migrants return with new skills and savings. These gains are often smaller than the loss of workers and of skills.

**Conclusion.** Large-scale emigration of the 18-60 age group tends to lower output and tax revenue and to deprive the country of skilled workers, although remittances and lower unemployment partly compensate.
